title: Ethics, Governance and Decisions Under Uncertainty
question: What do leaders owe the people their decisions affect, and how should they decide responsibly when their own judgment is biased and the consequences cannot be known?

overview.text: Executives are paid to decide things whose consequences fall on other people, often before the facts are in. This week asks what that responsibility requires. It brings together three bodies of thought that are usually taught separately: moral philosophy and corporate law on what organizations and their leaders owe; behavioral ethics on why decent people fail to see the ethical side of their decisions; and decision theory on how to act when the future cannot be forecast with honest probabilities.

Lesson 1 gives you four ethical questions to ask of any decision and maps the debate over whom organizations are for, with its sharpest form — accountability — in view. Lesson 2 explains bounded ethicality, ethical fading and the slippery slope, and holds that research to the course’s evidence standard, including a retraction at the heart of the field. Lesson 3 treats governance as the structures that keep decisions honest when individual judgment fails: agency costs, speak-up channels and the governance of predictive models. Lesson 4 is about deciding under deep uncertainty: robustness, precommitment and the special weight of irreversible decisions.

The Executive Dilemma places you inside a health network deploying a predictive model under pressure from a powerful sponsor. The case, The House Fund, puts you in a wealth manager where the founder’s own product is quietly favored. The assignment asks you to write the decision memo you would send in a situation like these. Week 12 covered how decisions become change; Week 14 covers how to defend a decision and learn from its outcome without hindsight. This week sits between them: deciding well, and responsibly, before anyone knows how it will turn out.

objectives: Apply consequentialist, duty-based, virtue and fairness questions to an organizational decision and identify where they diverge.
Evaluate competing accounts of corporate purpose and diagnose conflicts of interest and agency problems in a governance structure.
Explain bounded ethicality, ethical fading and the slippery slope, and weigh the supporting evidence according to its replication status.
Design governance for a predictive model, including its target variable, decision rights, validation and review triggers.
Choose and justify a decision strategy under deep uncertainty that accounts for robustness, irreversibility and who bears the downside.

lessons.title: What Executives Owe: Ethical Frameworks, Conflicts of Interest and the Purpose of the Organization
lessons.summary: Four ethical frameworks ask different questions of the same decision, and the debate over shareholder versus stakeholder purpose is really a debate about accountability.
objectives: Apply consequentialist, duty-based, virtue and fairness (contractualist) questions to the same organizational decision and explain where they diverge.
State the shareholder-primacy and stakeholder positions in their strongest forms, including the accountability critique of stakeholder governance.
Identify a conflict of interest and choose among disclosure, recusal, restructuring and prohibition as remedies.
lessons.executive: Ethical frameworks are not a menu from which to pick the one that blesses your preferred option. Use them as four independent tests: what are the consequences and for whom, what duties and rights are in play, what would a person of good character do, and could you justify the rule to everyone it affects. When all four agree, decide quickly. When they split, you have found the real dilemma, and your job is to choose openly and say what you are trading. On purpose, the shareholder–stakeholder debate is less about values than about accountability: a leader who answers to everyone can end up answering to no one. Whatever purpose you adopt, make it measurable and enforceable.

explore.text: Hypothetical. A consumer-lending startup has built a credit model that approves more applicants than its competitors at the same default rate. Its growth team has found a further gain: applicants who reach the final screen late at night accept higher-priced offers at much higher rates than daytime applicants. Nothing about this is illegal in the startup’s jurisdiction. Showing the higher-priced offer first at night would lift revenue materially in the next quarter, just before a funding round. The product lead calls it “time-of-day optimization”. A data scientist who built the analysis calls it “charging tired people more”. Both are describing the same table.

Before reading on, write one sentence that would justify launching the feature and one sentence that would justify refusing it. Which sentence was easier to write, and what does that tell you about the frame you started in?

This lesson does not tell you what to decide about the night-time pricing. It gives you four ways to examine the decision, a way to recognize when your own interests are bending your view, and a map of the larger argument about whom organizations are for. The rest of the week then asks why decent people miss ethical problems (Lesson 2), how organizations are governed so that they do not depend on individual virtue (Lesson 3), and how to decide when the consequences cannot be known (Lesson 4).

understand.text: Four questions, not one theory

Moral philosophy offers several families of theory. You do not need to choose one to be a competent executive, but you do need to know what each one notices and what each one tends to miss. APERTURE treats them as four independent questions to ask of any consequential decision.

**Consequences.** Consequentialist theories judge an action by its outcomes: who gains, who loses, by how much, and with what probability. This is the native language of management — cost–benefit analysis, net present value and expected value are consequentialist tools. Its strength is discipline about effects. Its weakness is that it can justify serious harm to a few people if the total gain is large enough, and it depends on predictions that are often biased toward the outcome the analyst prefers.

**Duties and rights.** Duty-based (deontological) theories hold that some actions are required or forbidden regardless of the total payoff: keep promises, tell the truth, do not use people merely as means, respect consent. In organizations these appear as fiduciary duties, confidentiality obligations, informed consent and contractual promises. Their strength is protecting individuals from being traded away. Their weakness is rigidity when duties conflict — the duty of confidentiality to one party against the duty to warn another.

**Character.** Virtue ethics asks what a person of practical wisdom, honesty and courage would do, and what this decision will make of the people who make it. Its strength is attention to habits and culture: organizations become what they repeatedly do. Its weakness is vagueness; two people can both claim to be acting with integrity and disagree.

**Fairness.** Contractualist and justice-based theories ask whether the rule behind a decision could be justified to everyone affected by it, especially those with the least power. A useful version is the publicity test: could you defend the rule if every affected party knew it? Its strength is surfacing the people who are absent from the meeting. Its weakness is that it gives limited guidance on how to weigh large benefits against small unfairness.

blocks.text: A **shareholder** owns equity in a corporation and holds residual claims: they are paid after creditors, employees and suppliers. A **stakeholder**, in R. Edward Freeman’s widely used definition, is any group or individual who can affect or is affected by the achievement of an organization’s objectives — employees, customers, suppliers, communities, regulators and shareholders among them. A **fiduciary** is someone legally bound to act in another’s interest; corporate directors and officers owe fiduciary duties of care and loyalty, which [Week 11](#w11-l4) covered. In most U.S. corporate law, those duties run to the corporation and its shareholders, but directors have wide discretion over how to pursue long-term value.

understand.text: Whom is the organization for?

Milton Friedman’s 1970 essay argued that business as such cannot have responsibilities; only people can. A corporate executive is an employee of the owners, and the executive’s responsibility is generally to make as much money for them as possible while conforming to the basic rules of society, in law and in ethical custom. An executive who spends the owners’ money on social goals they did not choose is, in Friedman’s argument, imposing a tax and deciding how to spend it without the accountability that governments face. The accountability point is the part of the essay most often forgotten.

Freeman’s 1984 book argued that strategy cannot be formulated well while attending only to owners, because many other groups shape whether the firm achieves its purpose. Managers should map their stakeholders, understand their stakes and power, and build processes for dealing with them. This began as a claim about good management and later became a family of normative claims about what managers owe.

In August 2019 the Business Roundtable, an association of chief executives of large U.S. companies, published a Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation signed by 181 of them. It committed to deliver value to customers, invest in employees, deal fairly with suppliers, support communities and generate long-term value for shareholders, replacing the group’s earlier position that corporations exist principally to serve shareholders.

Lucian Bebchuk and Roberto Tallarita responded that “stakeholderism” should be rejected even by people who care about stakeholders. Their argument is about incentives and accountability: corporate leaders’ pay and careers do not reward sacrificing shareholder value for stakeholders, so wider discretion is unlikely to help stakeholders, and a leader told to balance many constituencies becomes harder to hold accountable to any of them. Their review of companies whose chief executives signed the statement found little sign that governance documents changed, and they concluded the commitments were mostly for show. They argue stakeholder protection is better pursued through law, regulation and contracts.

The philosophical literature treats both positions as serious. Shareholder primacy is defended on grounds of property rights, clear accountability and the efficiency of markets constrained by law; stakeholder views are defended on grounds that law and prices fail to capture many harms, and that firms depend on relationships that a narrow objective can damage. Each side mixes empirical claims (what produces good outcomes) with normative ones (what is owed), and much confusion comes from not separating them.
Conflicts of interest

A conflict of interest exists when a person who has a duty to act for others also has a personal interest that could influence how that duty is performed. It is a structural condition, not an accusation: the conflict exists before anyone behaves badly. Agency theory explains why it matters. When an agent captures only part of the gain from serving the principal and all of the gain from serving themselves, interests diverge, and the principal bears costs — monitoring, bonding and a residual loss that never fully disappears.

items: **Disclosure** tells the principal about the conflict. It is cheap and sometimes sufficient, but research covered in Lesson 2 suggests people underestimate how much interests bend their own judgment, so disclosure alone rarely removes the bias.
**Recusal** removes the conflicted person from the decision. It works when someone else can decide competently.
**Restructuring** changes the incentive — paying an adviser a flat fee instead of a commission, or separating the person who builds a model from the person who validates it.
**Prohibition** forbids the conflicting interest or activity altogether, used where the stakes are high and monitoring is weak.

understand.caption: Legal and ethical are different axes
cells: Unlawful and indefensible: fraud, deliberate concealment. Rare in honest organizations, and not where most executive dilemmas live.
Lawful but hard to defend: the night-time pricing, exploiting a regulatory gap, burying a known defect within disclosure rules. The zone where most executive ethics happens.
Unlawful but arguably defensible: civil disobedience, refusing an order you believe is unlawful. Requires counsel and courage; rare in business.
Lawful and defensible: most decisions. The goal is to stay here deliberately rather than by accident.
understand.note: Original APERTURE teaching device. Law sets a floor; it rarely tells an executive what to do in the top-right cell.

challenge.text: **Frameworks can launder decisions.** Because four frameworks exist, a motivated decision-maker can usually find one that supports the preferred option and present it as “the ethical analysis”. The discipline is to run all four before you know which way you lean, and to write down where they disagree. A decision on which they split is a genuine dilemma; pretending otherwise is the error.

**Ethics is not only constraint.** Treating ethics as the list of things you may not do misses that many ethical failures are failures of omission — the safety concern no one raised, the analysis that was never commissioned because its answer might be inconvenient. Duties of care require effort, not only restraint.

The shareholder–stakeholder debate is unresolved. Bebchuk and Tallarita’s accountability critique is strong where stakeholder language is added without any mechanism for measurement or enforcement. Critics such as Colin Mayer reply that purpose can be written into governance with real accountability, and the philosophical literature notes that shareholder primacy depends on law and markets capturing harms that they often miss. Friedman himself bounded profit-seeking by law and ethical custom, which leaves open how much that boundary demands. A reasonable executive can hold either view; what is not reasonable is to hold both at once depending on which is convenient this quarter.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why the accountability argument has teeth

blocks.text: The core of the accountability critique is a measurement problem familiar from agency theory. A principal can monitor an agent only against objectives that can be observed. A single objective such as long-run shareholder value is imperfectly observable but at least has a common scale. A list of five constituencies with no rule for trade-offs lets an agent justify almost any decision by pointing to whichever constituency it helped. The agency literature predicts that more discretion with weaker monitoring raises agency costs.

The same logic applies inside organizations. A department told to “balance development, performance, wellness and cost” without a stated priority rule cannot be held to any of them. The remedy is not to abandon multiple objectives but to state the trade-off rule in advance, measure each objective and say who reviews the trade-offs.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the purpose statement and the bonus plan disagree

blocks.text: Your organization’s published values promise to “put people first”. The executive bonus plan pays only on revenue and cost. A manager asks which one she should follow when they conflict. You have five minutes and no time to redesign the plan. The honest answer is that incentives usually win, as [Week 2](#w02-l3) argued. What you can do now is name the conflict, decide which objective governs in this case and why, and write it down so the decision can be reviewed. The longer-term fix is to make the stated priority show up in what is measured and paid.

apply.text: **Worked example: the night-time pricing.** Run the four questions. Consequences: a revenue gain this quarter, a probable loss to borrowers who pay more than daytime applicants for the same risk, and a tail risk of regulatory attention and reputational damage if the practice becomes public. Duties: the company is not a fiduciary to borrowers, but it has a duty of honest dealing, and deliberately exploiting a known impairment of judgment sits uneasily with it. Character: the growth team will learn that targeting fatigue is acceptable. Fairness: the company would not publish the rule. Three of four questions point the same way. The financial case does not disappear; it is outweighed, and the memo should say so plainly.

Hypothetical, finance. An independent investment adviser receives higher compensation for recommending an in-house fund than for recommending an index fund with similar exposure. The conflict exists whether or not she ever recommends the in-house fund. Disclosure tells clients; restructuring to a flat advisory fee removes the incentive; recusal is impossible because she is the adviser. The strongest remedy is restructuring, because it changes the interest rather than relying on the client to discount the advice correctly.

Hypothetical, healthcare. A hospital department chair who holds equity in a device startup sits on the committee choosing which device to purchase. Disclosure to the committee is necessary but not sufficient. Recusal from the vote is the usual remedy, and the committee should also check whether the chair shaped the evaluation criteria before recusing.

In player development the clearest conflicts arise where an organization’s interest and a player’s interest diverge and the player depends on the organization’s advice: workload decisions near a promotion deadline, medical information that affects trade value, or a coach whose evaluation is tied to how prospects he championed perform. The fairness test is a practical tool: could you explain the rule you are applying to the player and his family, in his language, without embarrassment? Where you could not, restructure the decision — a second opinion that does not report to the same incentive, or a documented rule set before the case arises.

Pick one recurring decision in your work where your interest, your department’s interest and the interest of the person affected can diverge. Which of the four remedies — disclosure, recusal, restructuring, prohibition — does your organization actually use, and is it the right one?

retain.text: Ask four questions of every consequential decision — consequences, duties, character and fairness — before you know which way you lean. Agreement means decide; disagreement means you have found the dilemma and must choose openly. Whom the organization is for is a real debate, and its sharpest form is about accountability: an objective nobody can measure is an objective nobody can enforce. Conflicts of interest are structural conditions; remedies range from disclosure, which is weakest, to restructuring and prohibition.
Without looking back: what is the blind spot of the consequentialist question, and which framework most directly covers it?
State Bebchuk and Tallarita’s accountability argument in two sentences, then state the strongest reply.
Why is disclosure usually the weakest remedy for a conflict of interest?

takeaways: Use consequentialist, duty, character and fairness questions as independent tests; where they disagree, you have found the dilemma.
The lawful-but-hard-to-defend zone is where most executive ethics happens; law is a floor, not a guide.
Shareholder primacy and stakeholder theory are both defensible; the strongest critique of stakeholderism concerns accountability, not values.
A conflict of interest is a structural condition; restructuring incentives usually beats disclosure.

check.prompt: A hospital’s analytics team proposes publishing a new triage rule internally but not to patients, because “patients would misunderstand it”. Which framework question most directly challenges this choice?

options.text: The consequences question: what is the expected financial value of the rule?
Shareholder primacy: does the rule increase the owners’ returns?
The fairness (publicity) test: could the rule be justified to everyone it affects if they knew it?
Agency theory: what are the monitoring costs of the rule?

check.explanation: The fairness or contractualist question asks whether a rule could be defended to everyone it affects, and its practical version is a publicity test. A rule an organization is unwilling to disclose to the people it governs is a warning sign under that test. The other options may be relevant, but they do not address the secrecy itself.

optionFeedback.a: Consequences matter, but asking only about financial value ignores the issue raised: concealment from the people affected.
optionFeedback.b: Shareholder primacy concerns whom the firm serves; it does not speak to whether a rule can be justified to patients.
optionFeedback.d: Agency costs concern principals and agents; patients are not the principals monitoring the analytics team here.

check.prompt: Which statement best captures Bebchuk and Tallarita’s main objection to stakeholder governance?

options.text: Stakeholders do not deserve consideration from corporate leaders.
Stakeholder governance is illegal under U.S. corporate law.
Stakeholder theory has never been tested empirically.
Giving leaders discretion to balance many constituencies reduces their accountability and, given their incentives, is unlikely to help stakeholders much.

check.explanation: Their argument is about incentives and accountability: leaders are not paid to sacrifice shareholder value for stakeholders, and widening their mandate makes them harder to hold to account. They explicitly argue that people who care about stakeholders should prefer law, regulation and contracts.

optionFeedback.a: They say the opposite: people who care about stakeholders should reject stakeholderism because it will not protect them.
optionFeedback.b: Their argument is about policy and incentives, not illegality; directors have wide discretion under U.S. law.
optionFeedback.c: They examined what signatories of the 2019 statement actually did; their claim is not that the theory is untested.

lessons.title: Good People, Bad Calls: Bounded Ethicality, Ethical Fading and the Slippery Slope
lessons.summary: Most unethical organizational behavior is committed by people who do not experience themselves as choosing it; design for that, and hold the research behind it to the same standard you would hold any other evidence.
objectives: Explain bounded ethicality and ethical fading, and identify the four enablers of self-deception in a realistic decision.
Evaluate the evidence for the slippery-slope effect, distinguishing independently supported findings from retracted or unverified ones.
Design decision procedures that keep the ethical dimension of a decision visible.
lessons.executive: The main ethical risk in a well-run organization is not villains; it is decent people who stop seeing the ethical side of a decision. Euphemism turns “misleading customers” into “messaging”, small steps make the next one feel normal, and diffuse responsibility means nobody feels the decision was theirs. Design against this: name decisions in plain words, set bright lines before pressure arrives, treat the first small exception as the decision that matters, and assign someone to ask “who is harmed?” in the meeting. Be equally strict about the research: one well-known study in this field was retracted, so rely on findings that independent teams have reproduced.

explore.text: Hypothetical, technology. A software company’s quarterly sales report needs a number by Friday. In the first quarter, a regional manager books a deal two days early because the contract is “basically signed”. In the second, the finance team accepts a side letter that gives the customer an easy exit, because it is “standard flexibility”. In the third, the company counts a pilot as a full-year contract “in line with expected conversion”. By the fourth quarter, an auditor finds that revenue has been overstated for a year. Each person involved says, sincerely, that they never decided to misstate anything.
At which quarter did the problem begin? Who, if anyone, made an ethical decision? Write your answer before reading on.

The conventional view of ethics says people know right from wrong and choose. The sales story is uncomfortable because nobody seems to have chosen. Behavioral ethics, the field this lesson introduces, studies how ordinary cognitive processes let people take part in wrongdoing without experiencing an ethical choice — and what organizations can do about it.

understand.text: Bounded ethicality

Max Bazerman and Ann Tenbrunsel use the term **bounded ethicality** for systematic, often unconscious limits on people’s ability to act ethically, by analogy with bounded rationality. Their central observation is a gap that shows up at three moments. Before a decision, people predict that they will act ethically. At the moment of decision, a “want self” focused on immediate rewards takes over from the “should self” that made the prediction. Afterward, people remember their behavior as more ethical than it was. The result is that individuals and organizations consistently overestimate how ethical they are.

The same authors argue that people are poor at noticing unethical behavior by others when noticing it would be costly to them — when the person is a colleague, a source of revenue or a member of their group — and that informal culture and incentives frequently overpower formal ethics programs.
Ethical fading

Tenbrunsel and David Messick described **ethical fading**: the process by which the moral colors of a decision drain away, so that it is experienced as a business decision, a technical decision or a legal question rather than an ethical one. Once fading has occurred, people can act self-interestedly while believing their principles are intact. They identified four enablers of the self-deception that produces fading.

understand.text: Tenbrunsel and Messick drew a practical conclusion: because the problem is that people do not see the ethical issue, ethics training that teaches principles is likely to have limited effect. Interventions need to change how decisions are framed and structured so that the ethical dimension stays visible.
The slippery slope

David Welsh, Lisa Ordóñez, Deirdre Snyder and Michael Christian tested the slippery slope directly. Across four multi-round studies, participants who faced cheating opportunities that began small and grew gradually were more likely to commit the larger transgression than participants who faced the large opportunity abruptly. The effect operated through moral disengagement — small steps are easier to justify, and each justification lowers the bar for the next — and inducing a prevention focus weakened it.

understand.caption: How a slippery slope runs inside an organization

steps.label: Pressure
steps.text: A target, deadline or sponsor creates a reason to bend a rule a little.

steps.label: Small exception
steps.text: A minor, defensible-sounding step is taken, often with a euphemism.

steps.label: Rationalization
steps.text: The step is justified and becomes the new reference point.

steps.label: Normalization
steps.text: The next, slightly larger step now looks small by comparison.

steps.label: Discovery
steps.text: An outsider sees the cumulative distance; insiders still see only the last step.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what a “mechanism” and a “moderator” are

blocks.text: A **mechanism** (or mediator) is the process through which a cause produces its effect — here, gradual escalation increases cheating *through* moral disengagement. A **moderator** changes the strength of an effect — here, a prevention focus weakened it. The distinction matters for design. If you know the mechanism, you can target it directly; if you know a moderator, you know the conditions under which the problem is worst. Both claims need their own evidence, and both are weaker than the main effect if they come from a single study. [Week 4](#w04-l3) covers causal reasoning in more depth.

challenge.text: The research in this field has had its own integrity crisis, and it would be inconsistent to teach ethical blind spots while ignoring it. In 2012 a team including Bazerman and Francesca Gino reported in PNAS that signing an honesty pledge at the top of a form reduced dishonest reports compared with signing at the bottom, partly on the basis of a field study with an insurer. In 2020, the original authors and colleagues reported a large, preregistered direct replication and several conceptual replications that found no effect. In 2021, after independent analysts presented evidence that the field-study data were invalid, PNAS retracted the 2012 paper. Gino later became the subject of public data-integrity allegations about other papers, which she denies and has contested in court; Bazerman has written a book-length account of the affair from his side.

APERTURE’s policy is simple. **A retraction is a reported fact; a misconduct allegation is not a finding.** This course reports retractions and failed replications, and it does not adjudicate misconduct claims. **A finding earns weight when teams independent of the original authors reproduce it.** Under that rule, the actor-side slippery slope is supported by an independent team (Welsh and colleagues), although not yet by a large preregistered replication. Gino and Bazerman’s 2009 laboratory finding that observers tolerate gradual erosion in others’ behavior more than abrupt change is widely cited; we could not confirm whether that paper has been flagged, and until independent teams reproduce it, treat the observer version of the slippery slope as plausible but unverified. The signing-first effect should not be used.

Notice what this episode illustrates. The honesty-pledge idea was adopted by real organizations before it was replicated, because it was simple, cheap and appealing. Every mechanism in this lesson was at work: the attractive result faded the question of evidence quality, trust among collaborators substituted for verification, and each person could locate responsibility elsewhere. Your organization will face the same temptation with its own internal findings.

challenge.title: Methodological note: what the behavioral-ethics evidence can and cannot show

blocks.text: Most behavioral-ethics experiments measure small acts of cheating — over-reporting solved puzzles, misreporting a die roll — for small sums, usually with students or online participants. These designs give clean causal identification and poor ecological validity. Real organizational misconduct involves larger stakes, longer time scales, groups rather than individuals, and legal consequences. A laboratory effect can be real and still tell you little about its size in a finance department.

Two cautions follow. First, prefer findings with multiple independent studies and, ideally, preregistered replications; [Week 4](#w04-l2) explains why single studies with small samples overstate effects. Second, separate the conceptual insight from the effect size. That euphemism and gradualism make wrongdoing easier to rationalize is consistent with laboratory work, case histories and organizational research; that a particular nudge reduces cheating by a particular amount is a much stronger claim, and the signing-first case shows how such claims can fail.

apply.text: If the problem is that the ethical dimension disappears, the remedies are structural. None of them requires assuming bad intent.

items: **Name decisions in plain language.** Ban the euphemism in the decision memo: write “we will charge some customers more because they are tired” before you write “time-of-day optimization”. If the plain sentence is uncomfortable, discuss that discomfort.

**Set bright lines before the pressure arrives.** Rules agreed in calm conditions (“we never book revenue before signature”) are harder to erode one step at a time than case-by-case judgment under deadline.
**Treat the first exception as the decision.** Require the same review for a small exception as for a large one when it sets a precedent; the precedent is the real decision.
**Compare against the original baseline, not the last step.** A periodic review that asks how far current practice has drifted from the policy as written counters normalization.
**Assign the harm question.** Give one person in the meeting the explicit job of asking who is harmed and whether they would accept the rule.
**Reward early reporting.** People who raise small problems early must be visibly protected; otherwise the cheapest moment to stop a slide is lost (see [Lesson 3](#w13-l3)).

apply.text: Hypothetical, government. A transport agency’s safety inspectors have, over several years, extended the interval between bridge inspections “temporarily” each time the budget is tight. A new chief inspector asks for a chart of the actual interval over ten years against the written standard. The chart shows the drift that no single budget cycle made visible. The intervention is cheap, and it works on the mechanism — the comparison point — not on anyone’s character.

In player development, ethical fading tends to hide inside performance language. “Managing a player’s workload for roster flexibility” can mean protecting his health or obscuring that a decision serves the organization at his expense. “Aggressive assignment” can mean a development opportunity or exposure to injury risk he did not agree to. A practical habit for a department leader is to require that any decision affecting a player’s health, contract status or information privacy be written once in plain words — what we are doing, why, and who bears the risk — before it is discussed in the department’s usual vocabulary.

apply.title: Executive twist: the analyst who “cleaned” the data

blocks.text: Two days before an ownership presentation, you learn that an analyst removed several unfavorable observations from a chart as “outliers”, without a documented rule. The chart now supports the recommendation you have already circulated. No one has asked you about it, and the removal might be defensible. Under time pressure, every enabler is present: a euphemism (“cleaning”), a small step, diffuse responsibility and your own stake in the conclusion. The defensible move is to restore the observations, show both versions, state the rule you would apply and accept that the recommendation may weaken.

apply.text: Write down one euphemism common in your organization or industry. Translate it into plain words. Does the decision look different?

retain.text: Bounded ethicality means people predict, act and remember less ethically than they believe. Ethical fading drains the moral content from decisions through euphemism, gradualism, diffuse causation and self-image. The actor-side slippery slope has independent experimental support; the observer version and many specific nudges need independent replication, and the signing-first effect was retracted. The remedies are structural: plain words, bright lines, treating the first exception as the decision, and a fixed baseline.

takeaways: Most organizational wrongdoing is committed by people who do not experience an ethical choice; design for ethical fading rather than for villains.
Euphemism, gradual steps, diffuse causation and self-image are the four enablers to watch for.

lessons.title: Governance, Accountability and Responsible AI
lessons.summary: Governance is the set of structures that keeps decisions honest when individual judgment fails: agency costs explain why it is needed, speak-up channels show how problems surface, and model governance applies the same logic to algorithms.
objectives: Use agency-cost reasoning to diagnose a governance problem and choose among monitoring, incentive and structural remedies.
Explain why employees are central to detecting wrongdoing and what makes speak-up channels work.
Apply a model-governance sequence (govern, map, measure, manage) to a predictive model, including the choice of target variable.
lessons.executive: Governance exists because owners cannot watch agents, agents cannot watch themselves, and nobody sees everything. Three practical lessons follow. First, decide who decides, who reviews and who can stop a decision, and write it down before the hard case. Second, the people closest to the work see problems first; the evidence on corporate fraud says employees, not auditors or regulators, are among the most important sources of detection, so a speak-up channel is a control system. Third, a predictive model is a delegated decision-maker. Govern it like one: ask exactly what it predicts, who it affects, how it fails, who can override it and when it will be reviewed.

explore.text: In 2019 a team of researchers examined a commercial algorithm used by health systems to decide which patients should receive extra care-management help. The algorithm did not use race as an input, and it predicted what it was designed to predict quite well. Yet at the same risk score, Black patients were considerably sicker than White patients. The cause was the choice of target: the model predicted future health-care **costs** as a stand-in for health **needs**, and less money had historically been spent on Black patients with the same level of need.

Before reading on: whose job, in a hospital that bought this algorithm, was it to ask “what exactly is this predicting?” Write a job title. Then ask whether that person had the authority to stop the deployment.

This lesson treats governance as the answer to that question in general: structures that make someone responsible for asking, give them the information and authority to act, and hold them accountable for doing so.

understand.text: Why governance exists: agency costs

Michael Jensen and William Meckling defined an agency relationship as one in which a principal engages an agent to act on the principal’s behalf with delegated authority. When interests diverge, the principal bears **agency costs**: monitoring expenditures (audits, reporting, oversight), bonding expenditures by the agent (commitments that reassure the principal), and the residual loss that remains because monitoring is never perfect. A manager who owns a small share of the firm bears only a small share of the cost of shirking or self-dealing, so incentives diverge predictably.

The same structure repeats at every level. Owners delegate to executives, executives to department heads, department heads to analysts and coaches, and — increasingly — everyone delegates to models. Each delegation creates an information gap and a possible divergence of interest. Governance is the design of that delegation: who decides, on what information, under whose review, with what consequences.

rows: Monitoring
Make the agent’s behavior visible to the principal

Costly; monitors have their own agency problems

understand.title: Prerequisite: the duty of care is about process

blocks.text: In [Week 11](#w11-l4) you met the business judgment rule: courts generally do not second-guess directors’ business decisions, but they do examine whether directors informed themselves. In Smith v. Van Gorkom, the Delaware Supreme Court held directors liable for approving a merger after a brief meeting without adequate information. The lesson for governance is that accountability attaches to the quality of the process — what you knew, asked and documented — and not only to the outcome. Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice.

understand.text: Who sees problems first

Alexander Dyck, Adair Morse and Luigi Zingales studied a large sample of alleged frauds at large U.S. companies and asked who first brought each one to light. Detection relied less on the actors formally charged with oversight — investors, the SEC and auditors — than on employees, the media and industry regulators. They also found that whistleblowing is personally costly and that incentives and protections help explain who speaks.

The governance implication is direct. If the people closest to the work see problems first, then the quality of the channel from them to someone with authority is a primary control. A speak-up channel works when reports reach someone independent of the people reported on, when retaliation is credibly prevented, when reporters learn what happened, and when small problems are welcomed, not only large ones. The behavioral research in [Lesson 2](#w13-l2) adds a reason: because ethical fading makes insiders blind to slow drift, a channel that welcomes early, ambiguous concerns catches the slope while it is still shallow.
Models are delegated decisions

The healthcare algorithm study shows how bias can enter a model without any protected attribute as an input: through the choice of **label**, the thing the model is trained to predict. Because spending was a biased proxy for need, an accurate prediction of spending produced an unfair allocation of help. The researchers estimated that removing the disparity would raise the share of Black patients selected for extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%, and that retraining on direct measures of health rather than cost removed much of the bias.

understand.note: Figures as reported by Obermeyer et al. (2019) for the health system they studied.

understand.text: The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology’s AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, 2023) organizes this kind of work into four functions. **Govern** is cross-cutting: policies, roles, accountability and culture across the model’s life. **Map** establishes the context — intended use, affected people, possible harms. **Measure** assesses and tracks risks, including performance across groups. **Manage** prioritizes and acts on the risks, including decisions to deploy, limit or stop. The framework is voluntary and stresses that AI risks are socio-technical: they depend on how a system is used as much as on how it is built.

understand.caption: A model-governance sequence applied to any predictive tool (adapted from the four NIST AI RMF functions)

steps.label: Govern
steps.text: Name the owner, the validator (independent of the builder), who can override, who can stop it, and the review date.

steps.label: Map
steps.text: State the decision it informs, the exact target variable, who is affected, and what harm a wrong score causes.

steps.label: Measure
steps.text: Test accuracy overall and by relevant group; check whether the target is a biased proxy; test on data the builders did not see.

steps.label: Manage
steps.text: Decide: deploy, deploy with limits and human review, redesign the target, or do not deploy. Monitor drift and complaints.

challenge.text: **More oversight is not always better governance.** Every monitor is itself an agent. Review committees can become rubber stamps, compliance functions can optimize for documentation rather than safety, and a stack of approvals can diffuse responsibility until no single person feels accountable — the “errors in perceiving causation” enabler from Lesson 2 built into an org chart. Good governance gives each decision one clear owner and a small number of genuine checks.

**Fairness has more than one definition.** For predictive models, several reasonable statistical definitions of fairness — equal error rates across groups, equal selection rates, scores that mean the same thing for every group — generally cannot all be satisfied at once when base rates differ. Choosing among them is a value judgment, not a technical one, and it belongs to accountable decision-makers rather than being left to whoever writes the code.

**Human override is not a cure-all.** Adding a person who can override a model sounds safe, but people can defer to a score they do not understand, or override it selectively in ways that reintroduce bias. An override policy needs a record of overrides and periodic review of whether they improved decisions.

challenge.title: Methodological note: what the whistleblowing evidence can and cannot tell you

blocks.text: Dyck, Morse and Zingales could study only frauds that were eventually detected. Frauds that were never revealed are invisible, so the data cannot say what share of all wrongdoing employees catch, only who revealed the frauds that came to light. Their sample is large U.S. companies in a particular period, and later changes to whistleblower rewards and protections may have shifted the pattern. The robust lesson is qualitative — insiders see problems first and their incentives to speak matter — rather than any specific share.

The same selection problem applies to your own organization’s incident log. A falling number of reported concerns can mean fewer problems or a channel people no longer trust. Pair report counts with anonymous surveys asking whether people would feel safe raising a concern.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the sponsor owns the model and the review

blocks.text: A powerful executive commissioned a model, chose the vendor and will present its results to the board. He also proposes to chair the committee that validates it. Nobody disputes his competence. Under agency logic, the problem is structural: the person with the largest stake in the model’s success controls its review. You do not need to accuse anyone to propose that validation report to someone else; you need to frame it as standard practice that protects him as much as the organization.

apply.text: Hypothetical, finance. A regional bank adopts a vendor model to flag small-business loan applications for expedited approval. Mapping reveals that the model was trained on past approvals, so it predicts what loan officers approved, not which loans were repaid. Past approval decisions may embed the officers’ own biases. The governance response is to change the target to repayment where data allow, test performance across neighborhoods, require human review for declined applicants near the threshold, and set a review date.

Hypothetical, government. A city uses a model to prioritize building inspections. The model predicts past code violations, which depend partly on where inspectors chose to look. Without governance, the model sends inspectors back to the same neighborhoods, generating more recorded violations there and confirming itself. The fix is partly technical (some random inspections to measure true rates) and partly governance (someone accountable for checking the feedback loop).

Player-development organizations now run models that affect people directly: injury-risk flags that shape workload, projections that shape promotion and release decisions, and evaluation tools for amateur and international players who have little power and limited access to information. Each is a delegated decision. Ask the label question first: is the model predicting the outcome that matters (future major-league value, long-term health) or a convenient proxy (past playing time, which reflects past opportunity, or a scouting grade that may embed the scout’s preferences)? Then separate builder and validator, document who can override, keep player medical and biometric data under explicit access rules, and set a review date before the model goes live.

items: **Decision rights.** Write who recommends, who decides, who must be consulted and who can stop a model-informed decision ([Week 8](#w08-l2)).
**Separation.** The person who builds or champions a model should not be its only validator.
**Records.** Keep the version, data, target and validation results for each deployed model, and a log of overrides.
**Channel.** Make it easy for an analyst or coach to say “this model is wrong about this person” and have it reviewed.

lessons.title: Deciding When You Cannot Know: Deep Uncertainty, Robustness and Irreversibility
lessons.summary: When probabilities cannot be trusted, choose strategies that hold up across many futures, commit in advance to what will change your course, and treat irreversible decisions — especially those that affect other people — with a different standard of care.
objectives: Distinguish measurable risk from deep (Knightian) uncertainty and explain why expected-value maximization becomes fragile under the latter.
Apply robust and adaptive decision principles — scenarios, signposts, triggers and precommitment — to an organizational decision.
Classify decisions by reversibility and stakes, and explain the economic and ethical reasons for extra caution with irreversible decisions.
lessons.executive: Many of the decisions that define an executive’s tenure cannot be settled by an expected-value calculation, because nobody can honestly assign the probabilities. Do three things instead. First, ask which option performs acceptably across many plausible futures rather than best in the forecast you like. Second, write down in advance the signals that will change your course and what you will do when you see them; you will be less willing to change later. Third, sort decisions by reversibility. Move fast on reversible ones. Slow down on irreversible ones, especially when the people who bear the downside are not the people deciding.

explore.text: Hypothetical, public health. A health department must decide in early spring whether to buy a large stock of a vaccine for a new respiratory virus. If the virus spreads widely in autumn, the stock will save many lives and be worth its cost several times over. If it fades, the money is gone and the department will be accused of waste. Epidemiologists offer forecasts ranging from “almost certainly minor” to “severe” and cannot agree on how likely each is. The director is asked for “the probability of a severe season” so the finance office can compute an expected value.
Is there an honest number the epidemiologists can give? If you were the director, what would you ask for instead? Write two questions before reading on.

This lesson is about decisions like that one: consequential, partly irreversible, affecting people who are not in the room, and made under uncertainty that the available evidence cannot resolve. It builds on the valuation tools of [Week 10](#w10-l4) and the strategic options of [Week 9](#w09-l4), and it adds the ethical dimension that runs through this week.

understand.text: Risk and uncertainty

Frank Knight’s 1921 book distinguished **risk** — situations whose outcomes follow a known or estimable probability distribution, so that losses can be pooled and insured — from **uncertainty**, where each situation is sufficiently unique that no reliable distribution exists. Knight argued that profit is the reward for bearing uncertainty that cannot be insured, and that judgment in such situations is the distinctive function of the entrepreneur and the executive.

Later decision theorists argued that a rational person can always express beliefs as subjective probabilities, so Knight’s line is better treated as a spectrum than a wall. The modern literature on **deep uncertainty** takes a practical version of his point: decisions are deeply uncertain when the parties cannot agree on how the system works, on the probability distributions of key inputs, or on how to value the outcomes. Under those conditions, the edited volume by Vincent Marchau and colleagues argues, choosing the strategy that is optimal for a single best-estimate future is fragile; the better question is which strategy performs acceptably across many plausible futures and can be adapted as the future reveals itself.

understand.title: Prerequisite: expected value in one paragraph

blocks.text: The **expected value** of an option is the probability-weighted average of its outcomes. If an option pays 100 with probability 0.3 and loses 20 with probability 0.7, its expected value is 0.3 × 100 + 0.7 × (−20) = 30 − 14 = 16. Expected value is the right criterion when the probabilities are reliable, the decision is repeated many times so that averages are realized, and no single outcome is catastrophic. Each condition fails often in executive work: probabilities are guesses, the decision happens once, and some outcomes cannot be recovered from.

understand.caption: Why expected value becomes fragile under deep uncertainty

Experts disagree and estimates are biased toward the preferred option
Test the decision across a range of probabilities; ask at what probability it flips
The decision repeats, so averages are realized

understand.text: Robust and adaptive decisions

Marchau and colleagues present five approaches developed for deep uncertainty: Robust Decision Making, Dynamic Adaptive Planning, Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways, Info-Gap Decision Theory and Engineering Options Analysis. They differ in technique but share three ideas. Explore many plausible futures instead of one forecast. Seek strategies that perform acceptably across them, accepting some loss of performance in the most likely future in exchange for avoiding failure in the others. Build adaptation into the plan in advance: monitor **signposts** (indicators that tell you which future is unfolding) and specify **triggers** (thresholds at which pre-planned actions occur).

Robust Decision Making in particular reverses the usual analysis. Instead of asking “what will happen, and what is best given that?”, it asks “under what conditions would this strategy fail?”, and then judges whether those conditions are plausible enough to worry about. The question is the same one a premortem asks of a project.
Precommitment and the premortem

**Precommitment** means deciding in advance what you will do when a specified signal appears, and making that decision costly to reverse in the moment — the strategy of Ulysses tying himself to the mast. In organizations it takes plain forms: a written stopping rule for a pilot, a budget cap that requires board approval to exceed, a published review date for a model, or a rule that a deployment pauses automatically if a fairness metric crosses a threshold. Precommitment matters because, once a decision is made, sunk costs, reputation and the escalation tendencies covered earlier in this course make leaders reluctant to change course.

Gary Klein’s **premortem** is a practitioner technique for surfacing failure conditions before commitment: the team imagines that the decision has been implemented and has failed badly, and each member writes down why. Klein argues that this prospective hindsight legitimizes dissent and generates more specific risks than asking “what could go wrong?”. It is a practitioner heuristic rather than a rigorously tested intervention, and it pairs naturally with robust decision making: the premortem generates failure stories; the robustness analysis asks how plausible they are and whether a different strategy avoids them.
Irreversibility

Kenneth Arrow and Anthony Fisher showed that when an action is irreversible and information will improve over time, keeping options open has a value that a simple expected-value comparison misses. Ignoring that value biases decisions toward irreversible commitment. The idea, later called quasi-option value, is closely related to the real-options reasoning you met in finance.

understand.caption: Reversibility and stakes: matching the process to the decision
cells: Decide quickly, delegate, learn by trying. Most operational choices belong here.
Slow down enough to check the irreversible element; a short premortem; keep a record.
Move, but with monitoring and a fast way to undo it; tell those affected what you are trying.
Highest standard of care: independent review, robustness test across futures, precommitted triggers, consultation with or disclosure to those who bear the risk.
understand.note: Original APERTURE teaching device. Releasing personal data, ending a career, closing a facility and public statements are typical top-right decisions.

challenge.text: **Caution is not free.** The value of waiting depends on whether waiting will actually produce information, and delay can itself be irreversible: the vaccine not bought in spring cannot be bought in autumn. Treating every decision as irreversible produces paralysis, and organizations that cannot act under uncertainty cede ground to those that can. The matrix above is a sorting device; most decisions are reversible and should be made fast.

Daniel Kahneman and Dan Lovallo described a related pair of errors: “bold forecasts” produced by an inside view of a single project and “timid choices” produced by evaluating each risk in isolation, so that organizations reject individually risky but collectively attractive bets. Robustness reasoning should not become an excuse for timidity; it asks you to avoid unacceptable outcomes, not every loss.

**Robustness has its own subjectivity.** Someone chooses which futures count as plausible, what performance counts as acceptable and which strategies are compared. Those choices can be as biased as a probability estimate. The defense is the same as in any analysis: make the choices explicit, invite people with different views to add futures, and record why some futures were excluded.

challenge.title: Methodological note: does any of this improve decisions?

blocks.text: The evidence for deep-uncertainty methods is mainly case-based: Marchau and colleagues present applications in water management, infrastructure and climate adaptation, where they report that the methods clarified trade-offs and produced adaptive plans. Controlled comparisons of decision quality are rare, and the methods were designed for public-policy settings with modelling resources most organizations lack.

Reference-class forecasting, which you met in an earlier week, has stronger quantitative support for correcting optimism in project estimates, and it complements robustness thinking: the outside view widens the range of futures you take seriously.

The honest summary is that these are disciplined ways to think, supported by strong theory and practical experience, not interventions with measured effect sizes. Use them for their logic, and judge them by whether they change what your team considers.

apply.text: **Worked example: the vaccine decision.** Instead of a single probability, the director asks for three plausible autumn scenarios — minor, moderate, severe — and how each purchase option performs in each. Option A (full purchase) is costly in the minor scenario and life-saving in the severe one. Option B (no purchase) is cheap if minor and catastrophic if severe. Option C buys a partial stock now plus a contractual option to buy more by a fixed date, at a premium. Option C is not best in any single scenario but is acceptable in all three. The director then sets signposts (hospitalization data from the southern hemisphere’s season, early case growth) and a precommitted trigger: if a named indicator crosses a threshold by a set date, the option is exercised without further debate. The ethical lens adds that the people bearing the downside of under-buying are the most vulnerable residents, which argues for weighting the severe tail heavily.

Hypothetical, technology. A company considers publishing a large dataset of user interactions for researchers. The decision is irreversible: once released, data cannot be recalled, and re-identification techniques improve over time. A robustness question — under what future techniques would these users be identifiable? — and a stakes question — who bears the harm? — both point to the top-right cell of the matrix. A reversible alternative exists: provide access in a controlled environment with audit logs, which can be revoked.

Hypothetical, military. A logistics command must choose between consolidating supplies in one large depot (efficient in the expected case) or distributing them across several smaller sites (more costly, but resilient if one site is disrupted). The expected-value case favors consolidation; the robustness case favors distribution because the worst outcome of consolidation is unacceptable.

Player development is full of decisions with irreversible elements that fall on someone other than the decision-maker: releasing a player, signing an international amateur whose development will depend on your program for years, changing a pitcher’s mechanics or workload in ways that may affect his health, or sharing a player’s medical or biometric data with a partner. For these, write down the futures you considered (including ones you think unlikely), the signals that would tell you the decision is going wrong, the trigger that would make you change it, and who bears the downside if you are wrong. Reversible decisions — a drill, a practice schedule, a report format — deserve speed, not ceremony.

apply.title: Executive twist: the board wants one number

blocks.text: A board member asks, “What is the probability this works?” You do not have an honest single number. Refusing to answer looks evasive; inventing a number creates false precision. A defensible answer gives a range and its basis (“on comparable initiatives, somewhere between a third and two thirds succeed”), states what would move it, and then shifts to what you can promise: the conditions under which you will stop, the date of the first review and the worst outcome you have ruled out. That is a better commitment than a probability you cannot defend.

apply.text: Take a decision you expect to face in the next year. Place it in the reversibility–stakes matrix. Write one signpost and one precommitted trigger for it.

retain.text: Risk has reliable probabilities; deep uncertainty does not, and expected value becomes fragile when probabilities are guesses, decisions are one-off and some outcomes are ruinous. Robust and adaptive approaches ask which strategy performs acceptably across many futures and build in signposts, triggers and precommitment. Irreversibility has an economic value of flexibility and an ethical weight when others bear the downside; most decisions, though, are reversible and should be made quickly.

takeaways: Under deep uncertainty, prefer strategies that perform acceptably across many futures to strategies optimal for one forecast.
Write signposts and precommitted triggers before you commit; you will be less willing to change course later.
Irreversible decisions carry an option value of waiting and, when others bear the downside, a heavier ethical burden.
Most decisions are reversible: speed is the right response to them, not ceremony.
