glossary.definition: The family of ethical theories that judges actions by their outcomes — who gains, who loses and by how much. Cost–benefit analysis and expected value are consequentialist tools.
The family of ethical theories holding that some actions are required or forbidden regardless of total payoff, such as keeping promises, telling the truth and respecting consent.
A practical form of the fairness question: could you defend the rule behind a decision if everyone it affects knew it? Reluctance to disclose a rule is a warning sign.
The view that a corporation should be run in the interests of its shareholders, within the law and ethical custom, with executives acting as the owners’ agents.
In Freeman’s definition, any group or individual who can affect or is affected by the achievement of an organization’s objectives.
A situation in which a person with a duty to act for others has a personal interest that could influence how that duty is performed. It is a structural condition, not an accusation.
Systematic, often unconscious limits on people’s ability to act ethically, so that they predict, act and remember less ethically than they believe.

The process by which the ethical aspects of a decision recede from view, enabled by euphemism, gradual steps, diffuse causation and self-image, so the decision is experienced as merely technical or commercial.
The tendency for small, gradually escalating transgressions to lead to larger ones than an abrupt opportunity would, partly because each small step is easier to rationalize.
The costs that arise when an agent acts for a principal with divergent interests: the principal’s monitoring costs, the agent’s bonding costs and the residual loss that remains (Jensen and Meckling).
A variable a model predicts in place of the outcome that actually matters, such as health-care cost in place of health need. If the proxy is biased, an accurate model produces biased decisions.
Uncertainty that cannot be reduced to reliable probabilities because the situation is unique, as distinct from measurable risk (after Frank Knight, 1921).
A condition in which the parties to a decision cannot agree on how the system works, on the probabilities of key inputs or on how to value outcomes.
A signpost is an indicator that shows which future is unfolding; a trigger is a pre-set threshold on a signpost at which a pre-planned action is taken.
Deciding in advance what you will do when a specified signal appears, and making that choice costly to reverse in the moment.
The value of keeping options open when an action is irreversible and better information is expected, which a simple expected-value comparison omits (Arrow and Fisher).

exercise.title: Executive Dilemma

intro.text: You are the chief operating officer of Corbel Vale Health, a fictional non-profit network of outpatient clinics serving a mixed urban and rural region. Missed appointments cost the network money and lengthen waits for everyone. The chief executive has bought a vendor model that predicts which patients are likely to miss appointments, and he wants to use it to double-book those patients’ slots. Launch is three weeks away, and he has told the board it will close a third of the network’s operating deficit.

Five indicators move with your choices: **stakeholder trust** (patients, staff, community), **regulatory safety** (low legal and regulatory exposure; higher is safer), **mission** (equitable access to care, the network’s purpose), **financial position**, and **integrity** (whether what the organization does matches what it says). You will make four or five decisions with incomplete information. Every path trades some indicators against others, and no path is correct for every set of values. Before each choice, name which of this week’s four ethical questions you are relying on.

All people, organizations and numbers are fictional. Effects are ordinal teaching heuristics (−2 to +2) grounded in this week’s readings, not predictions of what would happen in a real health system. Nothing here is legal advice.

text.text: “The vendor says the model is 80 per cent accurate. We double-book the top fifth of predicted no-shows, starting in three weeks. Every month we wait costs us money we don’t have. I need you to own the rollout. Any questions?”

What you know: the vendor’s accuracy figure comes from other health systems. You have not seen which variables the model uses. Your clinic managers have not been consulted. The network’s data-governance policy requires a review for “new uses of patient data” but does not define the term.

choices.label: Commit to the three-week launch; ask the vendor for documentation in parallel.
choices.feedback: You protect the financial plan and the chief executive’s board commitment, but you are deploying a delegated decision-maker without knowing what it predicts or whom it affects. The undefined review requirement becomes something you chose not to trigger.

choices.label: Insist on a four-week review first: variables, accuracy by clinic and patient group, and what double-booking does to waits.
choices.feedback: You apply Map and Measure before Manage. The cost is a month of savings and some of the chief executive’s goodwill; the gain is knowing what you are deploying.

choices.label: Propose a limited pilot at two clinics, using the predictions for reminder calls and transport help instead of double-booking.
choices.feedback: You change the use rather than the model: a high score now triggers help rather than an overbooked slot. That reframes the decision but may not close the deficit the chief executive promised.

n2a.title: Week 5 — Two weeks after launch
n2a.speaker: Renata Osei, nurse manager, Hollin Street clinic (fictional)

text.text: “Double-booking is working on paper. But the people getting double-booked are mostly from the two rural routes and the east side — bus riders. When they do show up, they wait ninety minutes or get sent home. Two of my staff have started calling it ‘the bus penalty’. I’m not sure who I’m supposed to tell.”

choices.label: Quietly raise the score threshold so fewer patients are double-booked, and keep going.
choices.feedback: A quiet adjustment treats an equity problem as a tuning problem — a small step that makes the next one easier. It also leaves the nurse manager without an answer, which teaches staff that raising concerns changes little.

choices.label: Pause double-booking at the affected clinics and take the issue to the network’s ethics and compliance committee.
choices.feedback: You treat the nurse manager’s report as the governance signal it is. Insiders see problems first; how you respond determines whether they keep reporting.

choices.label: Ask analytics for a month of data before acting, so the decision rests on evidence.
choices.feedback: More evidence is reasonable, but a month of waiting while patients bear the cost is itself a decision. The analysis could run while double-booking is paused at the affected clinics.

text.text: “Two of the strongest predictors are prior no-shows and travel time to the clinic. Accuracy is close to the vendor’s figure overall, but double-booking based on it would add the longest waits to patients who already have the hardest time getting here. If we drop travel time, accuracy falls by a few points. The vendor contract has a penalty if we haven’t launched by next quarter.”
The chief executive has heard and is unhappy. “Every model has trade-offs. Are we running a clinic or a seminar?”

choices.label: Remove travel time and similar proxies, accept lower accuracy, and launch double-booking on the revised model.
choices.feedback: Removing a proxy is a reasonable step, but prior no-shows are themselves shaped by transport and work schedules. The use — double-booking — still concentrates the burden on patients least able to absorb it.

choices.label: Change the use: high scores trigger reminder calls and transport vouchers; double-book only where waits stay under a stated limit.
choices.feedback: You keep the model’s information and change what it does to people. Assistance rather than penalty fits the network’s mission; the financial case becomes uncertain.

choices.label: Defer to the chief executive and launch as planned; document your concerns in an email to him.
choices.feedback: Documenting dissent protects you more than it protects patients. Deferring to the sponsor when the sponsor also controls the review is the structural problem agency theory predicts.

text.text: “The pilot cut no-shows at the two clinics by a few points — real, but small, and the vouchers cost money. On these numbers we close maybe a tenth of the deficit, not a third. The chief executive wants to add double-booking for the very highest-risk patients. I can see both sides.”
The pilot ran for six weeks at two clinics, with no comparison group.

choices.label: Expand the assistance version network-wide and look for the rest of the savings elsewhere.
choices.feedback: You commit to the use most consistent with the mission on modest evidence. The financial gap is now your problem to solve, and the pilot had no comparison group, so the true effect is uncertain.

choices.label: Add double-booking for the top tier, with a cap on added waiting time and monthly monitoring by clinic.
choices.feedback: A bounded compromise: double-booking where it does least harm, with a monitoring rule. The cap and monitoring are only as good as the willingness to act when they show a problem.

choices.label: Commission an independent evaluation with a comparison group before scaling either version.
choices.feedback: You buy better evidence and separate the evaluator from the sponsor. The cost is time and the chief executive’s patience; the gain is a decision you can defend.

text.text: A local reporter has heard from patients that the network “books poor people into slots it expects them to miss”. She has a quote from a patient who lost half a day’s pay waiting. She asks whether Corbel Vale uses an algorithm to decide who gets double-booked and whether it has been checked for bias. Her deadline is tomorrow.

choices.label: Confirm the program, explain what it does, acknowledge the problem, and announce a pause and an independent review.
choices.feedback: Full disclosure under pressure is costly but consistent: the organization says what it does. Trust recovers more readily from an admitted problem than from one that is discovered.

choices.label: Issue a short statement: “We use industry-standard scheduling tools to improve access for all patients.”
choices.feedback: The statement is not false, but it is built to mislead — euphemism doing the work of a denial. It also creates a record that will be compared with internal documents later.

choices.label: Decline to comment until legal counsel reviews the program.
choices.feedback: Counsel’s review is prudent, but “no comment” reads as concealment and gives you no control of the story. Counsel can review a factual statement quickly.

n3b.title: Week 10 — The audit committee
n3b.speaker: Dr. Adaeze Brennan, chair of the board’s audit and compliance committee (fictional)

text.text: “I have read the analytics review. What I want to know is broader: how many other models does this network use, who approved them, and who checks them? Your chief executive tells me this one is under control. I would like to hear from you.”

choices.label: Recommend a network-wide model-governance policy: inventory, named owners, independent validation, fairness checks, review dates.
choices.feedback: You turn one incident into a system, which is what governance is for. It costs money and staff time, and the chief executive may see it as a rebuke.

choices.label: Describe the fix for this model and assure the committee the issue is resolved.
choices.feedback: Treating the problem as a one-off protects the relationship with the chief executive, but the committee asked a structural question and got a local answer. Other models remain ungoverned.

choices.label: Give a candid account, including that the sponsor of the model also controlled its review, and recommend that validation report to the committee.
choices.feedback: You name the structural agency problem without accusing anyone. The committee now has the information to act; your relationship with the chief executive will be tested.

text.text: “The assistance program is good news, and I want to announce it at the community health forum. Marketing has a headline: ‘Corbel Vale uses AI to eliminate bias in access to care.’ It will help us with donors.”
The model has not been audited for bias across all clinics, and the pilot evidence is modest.

choices.label: Agree: the program is good and the headline will raise money for it.
choices.feedback: Claims that outrun the evidence borrow against future trust. “Eliminate bias” is a claim no one can currently support, and it invites scrutiny.

choices.label: Propose an accurate announcement: what the program does, what the pilot found, what is still being tested, and when results will be published.
choices.feedback: You keep the announcement and remove the overclaim. Precommitting to publish results is a form of accountability that donors and patients can check.

choices.label: Ask that nothing be announced until the independent evaluation is complete.
choices.feedback: Silence avoids overclaiming, but it also forgoes a chance to build trust honestly, and staff who worked on the program may read it as a lack of support.

n4a.title: Week 16 — A letter from the regulator
n4a.speaker: Office of the state health department (fictional)

text.text: The state health department has received complaints about unequal waiting times and asks Corbel Vale to describe any automated tools used in scheduling, how they were evaluated and what the network knew about their effects. Internal emails, including the nurse manager’s concerns and any analytics review, may be requested. The chief executive suggests that “we keep the response tight”.

choices.label: With counsel, give a complete and accurate response, including what was known and when, and the corrective steps.
choices.feedback: A complete response under scrutiny is the point at which an organization decides what it is. It may cost money now and protects the network if documents surface later.

choices.label: Keep the response narrow and technically accurate, leaving out the internal concerns unless asked directly.
choices.feedback: Narrow answers that omit known concerns are where ethical fading becomes legal exposure. Internal documents usually emerge, and the omission becomes the story.

text.text: “The pause is costing us. The board is asking why we are behind on the deficit plan, and some of them think you went around me. I want double-booking back on at all clinics next month, with the fixes your team made.”
The independent review is half finished. Early results suggest that the revised model still produces longer waits for rural patients, though by less.

choices.label: Agree to restart, but only at clinics where the review shows no wait gap, with a precommitted stop rule if gaps appear.
choices.feedback: A bounded restart with a written stop rule respects both the financial pressure and the evidence. Its value depends on the stop rule being honored when it binds.

choices.label: Hold the pause until the review is complete and present the full results to the board yourself.
choices.feedback: Waiting for evidence protects patients and your integrity, but it escalates a conflict with your chief executive and leaves the deficit unaddressed for longer.

n5.title: Week 20 — Setting the rule for next time
n5.speaker: Dr. Adaeze Brennan, audit committee chair (fictional)

text.text: “We are adopting a policy for predictive tools. One question remains: who should have the final say on deploying a model that affects patients’ access to care?”

choices.label: The chief executive decides, after independent validation and a written equity review that goes to the committee.
choices.feedback: Clear decision rights with an independent check: the executive keeps authority, and the committee sees the evidence. Its strength depends on the validation being independent in fact.

choices.label: A standing committee including clinicians, a patient representative and compliance must approve each deployment.
choices.feedback: Broad participation builds legitimacy and surfaces harms early, but committees can slow decisions and diffuse responsibility unless one person remains accountable.

choices.label: Run a premortem on each proposed model, then let the sponsoring executive decide.
choices.feedback: A premortem surfaces risks, but leaving the decision with the sponsor reproduces the original agency problem: the person most invested in the model decides on it.

text.text: Corbel Vale ends the year with a governed scheduling program, a smaller reduction in its deficit than the chief executive promised, and a policy that applies to every model it uses. Some board members think you were too cautious; staff and the audit committee trust the process more. The question for you: what did caution cost, and who paid it?

The program caused real harm before it was corrected, and the network’s response to scrutiny was complete. The regulator closes its inquiry with recommendations. The episode costs money and reputation, and it leaves a record that the organization told the truth when it mattered. The question for you: at which earlier node could the harm have been prevented, and what would that have cost?

end-3.title: Outcome — The story that wrote itself

text.text: Internal emails reach the regulator and then the press. The story is no longer about a scheduling model; it is about what leaders knew and when. The financial savings are erased by legal costs and lost grants, and the nurse manager who raised the issue is now a public figure. Trace the path: how many of your choices felt, at the time, like small and reasonable steps?

You protected patients and the network’s integrity, and the evidence later vindicates your caution. But the deficit persisted, your relationship with the chief executive did not recover, and parts of the board see you as having worked around him. The question for you: was there a way to hold the line on the substance while keeping the sponsor inside the decision?

debrief.text: Every path in this exercise trades something real. Faster paths protect the financial plan and the chief executive’s commitment to the board and spend trust, mission and integrity; slower paths protect patients and the organization’s honesty and spend money and political capital. No ending is free.

items: **The first node mattered most.** Choosing to launch without mapping the model’s target and effects made later choices reactive. The NIST functions — govern, map, measure, manage — exist to make that first decision deliberate.
**The nurse manager was the governance system.** Insiders see problems first. Your response to her report determined whether the organization learned or drifted.
**Watch the euphemisms.** “Industry-standard scheduling tools”, “keep the response tight” and “eliminate bias” each did moral work disguised as communication.
**The sponsor problem was structural.** A chief executive who chose, championed and reviewed a model faces an agency conflict regardless of his intentions.

debrief.text: What the exercise does **not** show: how a real health system, regulator or press would respond. The indicator effects are teaching heuristics, the scenario compresses months into a few decisions, and real situations offer more options — including resigning or escalating outside the organization — than any branching tree can. Use your path as material for this week’s decision memo.

Compare your path with your stated values before you started. Which indicator did you protect without noticing, and which did you spend? Which of the four ethical questions — consequences, duties, character, fairness — did you lean on most, and where did they disagree? Then replay the exercise choosing differently at the first node and see how the later choices change.
Carry three ideas into the memo assignment: decide the use of a model, not only the model; treat early, ambiguous concerns as the cheapest moment to act; and write the stop rule before you need it.

assumptions: All people, organizations, figures and events are fictional.
Indicator effects are ordinal teaching heuristics (−2 to +2) derived from this week’s readings, not predictions or validated measurements.
“Regulatory safety” means low legal and regulatory exposure; it is not a legal assessment, and nothing here is legal advice.
The scenario assumes U.S.-style non-profit governance with a board audit committee; other structures would change the options.
Accuracy and savings figures quoted by characters are their claims, not verified facts.

case.title: The House Fund
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Numbers are synthetic and illustrative.

body.text: Brannock & Vey Wealth Partners manages money for about four thousand households, most of them retired teachers, nurses and small-business owners in three neighboring states. The firm was founded twenty-two years ago by Desmond Vey, who still runs it and owns 61 per cent of its shares. Its reputation rests on a simple promise printed on every client statement: “We are paid by you, and only by you.”

Five years ago the firm launched its own fund, the Brannock & Vey Core Income Fund, managed by an affiliated company in which Vey and two other partners hold a majority stake. The house fund has performed respectably. It also charges more than the index funds the firm had previously used for the same role in client portfolios, and the affiliated manager’s fee flows, indirectly, to the same partners who set the firm’s portfolio policy. The relationship is disclosed in a paragraph on page 14 of the firm’s regulatory brochure.

Ines Takahara joined the firm eighteen months ago as a portfolio analyst. In March she was asked to rebuild the model-portfolio tool that advisers use to generate recommendations. While testing it, she noticed that the tool’s optimizer contained a constraint she had not seen documented: for clients classified as “income-oriented”, it set a minimum allocation of 25 per cent to the Core Income Fund, regardless of what the optimizer would otherwise have chosen. Without the constraint, the optimizer allocated between zero and 8 per cent to the house fund for those clients, preferring two lower-cost index funds with similar holdings.

Takahara pulled five years of data (Exhibit 1). After fees, the house fund had trailed the blended index alternative by an average of 0.6 percentage points a year, although it had beaten the alternative in two of the five years and had slightly lower volatility. Across the roughly 1,900 client households affected, she estimated the cumulative shortfall at between $9 million and $14 million, depending on assumptions about rebalancing and timing. She was careful to label the estimate rough.

She took the spreadsheet to her manager, the head of investment research, Calloway Mensah. Mensah looked at it for a long time. “The constraint was added when the fund launched,” he said. “I was told it was there for diversification and to give the fund scale. I didn’t design it.” He thanked her, asked her not to circulate the analysis, and said he would “take it upstairs”.

Mensah brought the issue to you. You are the firm’s chief operating officer, a non-partner executive hired three years ago from a larger asset manager, and you chair the internal risk committee. You report to Vey. Mensah wants your advice before he says anything to Vey, because Vey personally championed the house fund and regards criticism of it as criticism of the firm.

You read the analysis twice. Several things are unclear. The general counsel, Priya Raman, is on leave for two weeks; her deputy is competent but junior. You do not know whether the constraint was ever approved by the investment committee, whose minutes from five years ago are thin. You do not know whether advisers knew the constraint existed or simply trusted the tool. The firm’s disclosure says it “may recommend affiliated funds” and that this “creates a conflict of interest”; it does not say the model tool forces a minimum allocation. Whether that difference matters legally is a question for counsel. Whether it matters ethically is a question for you.

The financial stakes for the firm are real. The house fund accounts for about a fifth of the firm’s revenue once the affiliated manager’s fees are counted, and the firm is in the middle of negotiations to sell a minority stake to a private-equity investor. Vey has told the leadership team that the valuation depends on “stable, growing revenue lines”.

On Tuesday you meet Vey. You describe the constraint and the analysis without characterizing anyone’s intent. He listens, then says: “The fund has done fine. Two of five years it beat the index. Volatility is lower. Our clients are retirees; lower volatility is worth something to them. The disclosure covers it. And I’m not going to blow up the investor process over a 60-basis-point difference that an analyst estimated with a spreadsheet.” He suggests that the research team “refine the analysis” over the next quarter and that the constraint be “reviewed as part of the normal annual process”.

On Wednesday the deputy general counsel tells you, informally, that the disclosure “is arguably adequate, but arguably isn’t”, that regulators have taken a strong interest in undisclosed constraints that favor affiliated products, and that if the firm decides to remediate it should do so with counsel involved from the start. He adds that anything written now may be read later by a regulator or in litigation, and that is a reason to write carefully, not a reason not to write.

On Thursday Takahara asks to see you. She is polite and nervous. She has heard nothing since she gave Mensah the spreadsheet. She says that if the firm does not act she is unsure what her own obligations are, and asks whether the firm has a confidential reporting channel. It has one, an outsourced hotline set up four years ago; as far as you know, it has received two reports, neither substantive.

The board, which consists of Vey, two other partners and two independent directors, meets in ten days. The independent directors are a retired bank examiner and the former chief executive of a regional hospital. The private-equity investor’s due diligence team has asked for a list of “any known compliance matters”.

You see at least four options. You could support Vey’s proposal: remove nothing now, commission a fuller analysis, and review the constraint in the annual process. You could remove the constraint immediately for new allocations, quietly, and let existing portfolios drift back toward the optimizer’s recommendations at the next rebalancing. You could take the issue to the board, including the independent directors, with a recommendation to remove the constraint, retain outside counsel, assess client harm properly and consider restitution and disclosure to clients and the regulator. Or you could escalate further — for instance by insisting the issue be disclosed to the investor’s due diligence team before the board meets.

Each option has costs you can name and costs you cannot. Removing the constraint will reduce revenue and may affect the sale. Disclosure may invite regulatory scrutiny of matters beyond this one. Restitution, if it is owed, could be large, and its size depends on assumptions nobody has yet tested. Not acting carries the risk that the analysis is right, that clients have been harmed, and that the firm’s promise on every statement has become untrue. It also carries a quieter risk: Takahara, Mensah and you now know, and what you each do next will shape what everyone in the research team believes about what the firm’s values mean in practice.
You have scheduled thirty minutes with Vey on Monday. You want to arrive with a recommendation, a plan for the next ten days and a clear view of what you will do if he disagrees.

questions: Apply the four ethical questions (consequences, duties, character, fairness) to Vey’s proposal and to the option of going to the full board. Where do they agree and where do they split?
Identify every conflict of interest in the case, including your own. Which remedy — disclosure, recusal, restructuring, prohibition — fits each?
Which enablers of ethical fading are visible in the conversations, and how would you counter them in the way you write your recommendation?
What can be decided now, and what should wait for better information? Write one signpost and one precommitted trigger for the part that waits.
What do you owe Ines Takahara, and what will the research team learn from how this is handled?

perspectives.title: Go to the full board now
perspectives.text: The firm owes fiduciary duties to clients, and the constraint was not disclosed in the form it took. The independent directors exist precisely for decisions in which the founder is conflicted. Remove the constraint for new allocations immediately, retain outside counsel, commission an independent harm analysis, and let the board decide on restitution and disclosure. The investor process is a reason to act, not to wait: a known issue that surfaces after closing is far worse. Cost: conflict with the founder, revenue loss and possible regulatory attention.

perspectives.title: Act now, decide restitution later
perspectives.text: The facts about harm are uncertain, and an analyst’s spreadsheet is not a finding. But the constraint itself is the problem, regardless of the harm estimate. Remove it now (a reversible, low-regret step), document the decision with counsel, and give the board a ten-day plan for establishing the facts before deciding on restitution and external disclosure. This separates the reversible decision from the irreversible ones. Risk: it can look like a quiet fix if the board is not told fully.

perspectives.title: Support a structured review, with conditions
perspectives.text: Vey’s points about volatility and two winning years are not frivolous, and a rushed disclosure could harm clients by triggering costly reactions to an estimate that may be wrong. Agree to a review, but not the “normal annual process”: a thirty-day independent analysis reporting to the independent directors, the constraint suspended for new money in the meantime, and a written trigger for disclosure if harm exceeds a stated threshold. This keeps the founder inside the decision. Risk: it can become the first step on a slippery slope if the conditions are not honored.

case.application: Player-development organizations face the same structure whenever a leader’s own project shapes how people are treated: a development program that a senior executive championed and that the organization’s tools quietly favor, a measurement system built by the person whose results it evaluates, or a medical or workload policy that serves the club’s roster interests at a player’s expense. The case’s questions transfer directly — who designed the constraint, who knew, what is disclosed to the people affected, who reviews it independently — and so does the hardest one: what you do when the person who must approve the fix is the person most invested in the status quo.

questions.prompt: Which response best applies this week’s approach to ethical frameworks?

stimulus.text: Fictional. A city transit agency can save money by ending late-night bus service on two routes. Ridership is low, but the riders are mostly night-shift hospital and warehouse workers with no car. The finance director’s memo concludes: “On a cost–benefit basis this is clearly correct, so there is no ethical issue.”

options.text: Accept the memo: cost–benefit analysis is the ethical analysis for a public agency.
Reject the memo: any decision that harms vulnerable people is unethical.
Defer the decision until riders vote on it.
Ask the duty, character and fairness questions as well; if they point the other way, the agency faces a genuine dilemma that should be decided openly rather than defined away.

questions.explanation: The memo uses one framework and declares the question closed. The week’s approach runs all four questions independently. The fairness question — could the rule be justified to night-shift workers who depend on the bus? — may disagree with the cost–benefit result. Disagreement does not settle the answer; it means the trade-off must be stated and owned.

optionFeedback.a: Cost–benefit analysis is a consequentialist tool, and its blind spot is harm concentrated on a few people; treating it as the whole analysis is the error.
optionFeedback.b: Almost every decision harms someone; an absolute rule makes most public decisions impossible and skips the weighing that is required.
optionFeedback.c: Consultation can be valuable, but a vote of affected riders is not a decision rule the agency can adopt for every service change, and it avoids the agency’s own responsibility.

questions.prompt: Select every conflict of interest present in this situation.

stimulus.text: Fictional. A hospital’s chief medical officer chairs the committee selecting a new surgical robot. Her spouse is a paid consultant to one vendor. The committee’s evaluation criteria were drafted by a surgeon who trained on that vendor’s robot and prefers it. The hospital’s chief financial officer will receive a bonus if capital spending stays under budget this year. A patient advocate on the committee has no financial ties to any vendor.

options.text: The chief medical officer’s spouse is paid by a bidding vendor.
The chief financial officer’s bonus is tied to capital spending, which this purchase affects.
The surgeon who drafted the criteria prefers the robot he trained on.
The patient advocate has no financial ties to any vendor.
The committee is chaired by a physician rather than an administrator.

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest exists when a person with a duty to act for others has a personal interest that could influence that duty. The spouse’s consulting income and the CFO’s bonus are personal interests tied to the decision. The surgeon’s training-based preference is a familiarity bias worth managing (for example, by having criteria reviewed), but it is not a personal interest in the usual sense. The advocate’s independence and the chair’s profession are not conflicts.

questions.prompt: What is the central flaw in this reasoning?

stimulus.text: Fictional board memo: “Our company signed a statement committing to serve customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders. We therefore no longer need performance targets tied to shareholder returns in executive pay. Our leaders will balance all constituencies using their judgment, and the board will review whether they did so.”

options.text: Stakeholder statements are illegal for public companies.
It fails to compute the net present value of each stakeholder group.
It removes a measurable objective without replacing it with any measurable trade-off rule, making leaders harder to hold accountable to any constituency.
Employees are not stakeholders under Freeman’s definition.

questions.explanation: This is the accountability problem Bebchuk and Tallarita emphasize: a list of constituencies with no priority rule lets almost any decision be justified by pointing to someone it helped. The fix is not necessarily shareholder primacy; it is stating measurable objectives and trade-off rules for whatever purpose the firm adopts.

optionFeedback.a: Such statements are not illegal; the problem is governance design, not legality.
optionFeedback.b: Net present value per stakeholder group is not a meaningful requirement; the issue is accountability.
optionFeedback.d: Employees are central stakeholders in Freeman’s definition.

questions.prompt: How should a compliance team weigh this evidence before redesigning its expense forms?

stimulus.text: Fictional research summary prepared for a compliance team:

stimulus.caption: Evidence on a proposed “honesty pledge” intervention (fictional summary modelled on a real pattern)
rows: Original paper (Year 1)
Two lab studies and one field study with a company partner
Pledge at the top reduced over-reporting
Replication (Year 9)
Preregistered direct replication, large sample, partly the same authors
No effect
Journal notice (Year 10)
Original field data found invalid
Original paper retracted

options.text: Do not rely on the pledge: the original is retracted and a large preregistered replication found no effect; look for interventions with independent replicated support.
Adopt the pledge: two lab studies still support it, and it costs nothing.
Average the original and replication effects to get a moderate effect size.
Treat the evidence as balanced, one study for and one against.

questions.explanation: A retracted paper no longer counts as evidence, and a high-powered preregistered replication finding no effect is strong evidence against the claim. The pattern mirrors the [signing-first case](R-shu-2012-signing) and its [failed replication](R-kristal-2020-signing). Under the course’s policy, findings earn weight through independent replication.

optionFeedback.b: The lab studies were part of a retracted paper, and the replication failed; “costs nothing” ignores the cost of a false sense of control.
optionFeedback.c: You cannot average a retracted result with a valid one; the retracted data are not evidence.
optionFeedback.d: A retracted study and a preregistered high-powered replication are not equal weights.

questions.prompt: Which intervention most directly targets the slippery-slope mechanism described by Welsh and colleagues?

options.text: An annual ethics lecture on the firm’s values.
A larger bonus for meeting quarterly targets.
A personality test for new hires that screens for integrity.
A rule that any exception setting a precedent receives the same review as a large exception, and a periodic comparison of practice with the original written policy.

questions.explanation: The slippery slope works because each small step is judged against the previous step, and small steps are easy to rationalize. Reviewing precedent-setting exceptions and comparing practice with a fixed baseline counter both features. Tenbrunsel and Messick’s analysis predicts that training alone will do little, and selection does not change the situation.

optionFeedback.a: Teaching principles does not keep the ethical dimension visible at the moment of decision.
optionFeedback.b: Stronger target incentives increase the pressure that starts a slope.
optionFeedback.c: Character screening assumes the problem is bad people; the research suggests ordinary people slide under gradual pressure.

questions.prompt: You lead a data team. An analyst tells you, informally and uncertainly, that a revenue forecast the CEO has already presented may rest on a double-counted customer. Which first move is best?

options.text: Wait until the analyst is certain before raising it, to avoid embarrassing the CEO with a false alarm.
Correct the forecast quietly in the next version without mentioning the error.
Thank the analyst, verify the specific claim quickly, and tell the CEO what you know and when you will know more — while making clear the analyst did the right thing.
Report the analyst’s concern to the board directly, bypassing the CEO.

questions.explanation: Early, ambiguous concerns are the cheapest moment to act, and how leaders respond decides whether insiders keep reporting. Quick verification plus prompt, calibrated communication respects both accuracy and the CEO’s need to know. Escalation outside the chain is for when the normal channel fails or is conflicted.

optionFeedback.a: Waiting for certainty lets the error compound and teaches analysts that uncertain concerns are unwelcome.
optionFeedback.b: A quiet correction is a small step down a slope and leaves the CEO having presented a wrong number.
optionFeedback.d: Bypassing the CEO before verifying a routine error is disproportionate; it is the right move only if the normal channel is conflicted or fails.

questions.prompt: A bank is about to deploy a vendor model that predicts which small-business applicants to fast-track. Rank these governance steps in the order they should happen.

options.text: Measure accuracy and error rates by neighborhood and business type on data the vendor did not see.
Name an owner, an independent validator, who can override and who can stop the model.
Decide whether to deploy, deploy with limits and human review, or redesign.
Establish exactly what the model predicts (past approvals or repayment) and who is affected.

questions.explanation: The sequence follows Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. Accountability comes first so that later findings have someone to act on them; mapping the target and affected people determines what to measure; measurement informs the deployment decision. Govern is cross-cutting, but naming roles before analysis begins prevents the sponsor from controlling the review.

questions.prompt: In the healthcare algorithm studied by Obermeyer and colleagues, what was the main source of racial bias?

options.text: The model predicted health-care costs as a proxy for health needs, and less was spent on Black patients with the same needs.
Race was used as an input variable.
The training sample contained too few patients.
Clinicians overrode the model’s recommendations in biased ways.

questions.explanation: The bias came from the label: cost was a biased proxy for need. The model predicted cost well, so accuracy did not reveal the problem. Retraining on health measures rather than cost substantially reduced the bias.

optionFeedback.b: The study emphasizes that race was not an input; bias entered through the target.
optionFeedback.c: Sample size was not the identified problem.
optionFeedback.d: The analysis concerned the algorithm’s scores, not clinician overrides.

questions.prompt: A league office is choosing a new tiebreak format. Option A gains 10 (units of value) if fans respond well and loses 30 if they respond badly. Experts disagree: estimates of the probability that fans respond well range from 0.6 to 0.9. At what probability of a good response does Option A’s expected value equal zero? Give a decimal.
questions.working: Expected value = p × 10 + (1 − p) × (−30) = 10p − 30 + 30p = 40p − 30. Setting 40p − 30 = 0 gives p = 0.75. Because the experts’ range (0.6 to 0.9) straddles 0.75, the sign of the expected value depends on which expert is right — a signal to look for a more robust option or to stage the decision.
questions.explanation: The break-even probability is 0.75. Finding the probability at which a decision flips is more useful under deep uncertainty than computing expected value at a single guess: here the plausible range includes both positive and negative expected values, so the decision is not robust.

questions.prompt: Which features make a decision belong in the “highest standard of care” cell of the reversibility–stakes matrix? Select all that apply.

options.text: Its effects cannot be undone once made.
People other than the decision-maker bear much of the downside.
It is made frequently, so averages will be realized.
It concerns a report format that can be changed next week.
Information that would improve the decision is likely to arrive later.

questions.explanation: Irreversibility and stakes for others define the cell, and expected future information adds an option value of waiting (Arrow and Fisher). Frequent decisions and easily changed formats belong in the reversible, fast-decision cells.

questions.prompt: An organization you know (or a hypothetical one) is about to use a predictive score to make decisions about people who have little power over the result — employees, patients, players or applicants. In 150–250 words, recommend whether and how it should proceed. Use at least two ethical frameworks, name the agency or governance risk, and include one precommitted trigger.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer states a recommendation first (for example, “deploy in a limited form with assistance rather than penalties, after an independent validation”). It applies two frameworks explicitly — for instance, consequences (who gains and who bears error costs, including concentrated harms) and fairness (could the rule be explained to the people scored?) — and says where they agree or diverge. It identifies a governance risk such as the sponsor validating their own model, or a target variable that is a biased proxy, and proposes a structural remedy (independent validator, named override authority, review date). It includes a precise trigger, such as “pause if the error rate for any group exceeds the overall rate by a stated margin for two consecutive months”, and notes what remains uncertain.

levels: 0 — No clear recommendation or no framework named
1 — Recommendation present; one framework or superficial use of two
2 — Clear recommendation; two frameworks applied and their agreement or tension stated
1 — Risk named without a structural remedy
2 — Specific agency or target-variable risk with a structural remedy
2 — Specific, observable trigger with a pre-agreed action

reserve.prompt: Which statement about Friedman’s 1970 essay is most accurate?

options.text: It argued that firms should maximize profit by any means, including deception.
It argued that corporations are moral persons with their own social responsibilities.
It argued that executives act as agents of the owners and should pursue profit within the law and ethical custom, and that spending owners’ money on social goals lacks democratic accountability.
It argued for the stakeholder approach later developed by Freeman.

reserve.explanation: Friedman bounded profit-seeking by law and ethical custom and grounded his position in agency and accountability. The common caricature — profit by any means — ignores those limits.

optionFeedback.a: Friedman explicitly excluded deception and fraud.
optionFeedback.b: Friedman argued the opposite: only people have responsibilities.
optionFeedback.d: Freeman’s stakeholder approach is the principal alternative to Friedman’s view.

reserve.prompt: “The model recommended it, and legal signed off.” Which enabler of ethical fading does this sentence most clearly express?

options.text: Euphemistic language
The slippery slope
Quasi-option value
Errors in perceiving causation (diffused responsibility)

reserve.explanation: Locating responsibility in a model and another department diffuses causation, so no one experiences the decision as their own. That is the causation enabler.

optionFeedback.a: No euphemism is used; the sentence relocates responsibility.
optionFeedback.b: Nothing suggests a gradual series of steps.
optionFeedback.c: Quasi-option value is an economic concept about irreversibility.

reserve.prompt: What does the Dyck, Morse and Zingales evidence most directly suggest the CFO should do?

stimulus.text: Fictional. A mid-sized manufacturer’s CFO wants to reduce fraud risk. Options: double the external audit budget, or invest the same amount in a confidential reporting channel with independent review, protection from retaliation and feedback to reporters.

options.text: Seriously consider the reporting channel, because employees are among the most important sources of fraud detection, and their incentives and protections matter.
Double the audit budget, because auditors are the main detectors of fraud.
Neither, because fraud cannot be detected before it is reported in the media.
Rely on the regulator, which detects most frauds.

reserve.explanation: The study found that detection relied less on auditors and regulators like the SEC and more on employees, media and industry regulators. A credible internal channel targets the group closest to the work. The evidence does not say audits are useless; it says the channel deserves investment.

optionFeedback.b: Auditors were not the leading source of detection in that study.
optionFeedback.c: Employees often detect fraud before it reaches the media.
optionFeedback.d: The SEC was not among the leading sources of detection in that study.

reserve.prompt: A city must choose a flood-protection plan. Forecasts of sea-level rise by 2060 vary widely and experts cannot agree on probabilities. Which approach best fits deep-uncertainty guidance?

options.text: Build to the single most likely forecast, because that maximizes expected value.
Build for the worst imaginable case regardless of cost.
Wait until the uncertainty is resolved.
Choose a plan that performs acceptably across many plausible futures, with signposts and pre-planned triggers for adding protection.

reserve.explanation: Robust and adaptive approaches seek acceptable performance across futures and build in signposts and triggers so the plan can change as the future reveals itself. Optimizing for one forecast is fragile; building for the extreme is wasteful; waiting may itself be irreversible.

optionFeedback.a: Optimizing for a single forecast is fragile when the forecast is deeply uncertain.
optionFeedback.b: Robustness avoids unacceptable outcomes; it does not require paying any price to avoid every loss.
optionFeedback.c: The uncertainty may never be resolved in time, and delay can itself be irreversible.

assignment.title: Executive decision memo on an ethical or governance dilemma

brief.text: Write a decision memo to a senior decision-maker — a chief executive, a board committee or an owner — on a hypothetical, non-confidential dilemma with competing obligations and incomplete information. You may use the House Fund case, your own path through the Executive Dilemma, or a scenario you construct. If you build your own, keep it fictional: no real organization, colleague, player or confidential information.

The memo must lead with a recommendation, separate what is known from what is not, name the people and obligations at stake, compare real options, analyze them through at least two of this week’s ethical frameworks, state the strongest counterargument, identify potential harms and safeguards, and say how and to whom the decision will be disclosed and when it will be reviewed.

items: Write for a reader with ten minutes who must decide.
Plain words for every decision: if a sentence relies on a euphemism, rewrite it.
Separate reversible from irreversible parts of the decision.
Educational exercise only: if your scenario raises legal questions, flag them for counsel rather than resolving them.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,300-word executive decision memo with a recommendation, analysis through at least two ethical frameworks, risks under uncertainty, a disclosure plan and review triggers.

template.heading: Recommendation
template.guidance: Two or three sentences: what you recommend, the main reason and the most important condition.

template.heading: Facts and unknowns
template.guidance: What is established, what is disputed, what is unknown, and how and when each unknown could be resolved.

template.heading: Stakeholders and obligations
template.guidance: Who is affected, what each is owed (legal, contractual, ethical) and any conflicts of interest, including your own.

template.heading: Options
template.guidance: Three or four genuine options, including one you do not favor, with what each costs and protects.

template.heading: Analysis through two or more frameworks
template.guidance: Apply at least two of consequences, duties, character and fairness. Say where they agree and where they split, and how you resolve the split.

template.heading: Counterargument, harms and safeguards
template.guidance: The strongest case against your recommendation, the harms your recommendation could cause and the safeguards that limit them.

template.heading: Risks under uncertainty
template.guidance: How the recommendation performs across plausible futures, which elements are irreversible and who bears the downside if you are wrong.

template.heading: Disclosure, implementation and review triggers
template.guidance: Who will be told what and when; the first implementation steps; signposts, precommitted triggers and the review date.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Clear recommendation in the opening sentences with its key condition; every section serves the decision; readable in ten minutes.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Recommendation is clear and early; minor digressions.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Recommendation appears late or is hedged so heavily that the reader cannot act on it.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No identifiable recommendation.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Known, disputed and unknown facts clearly separated with a plan to resolve key unknowns; stakeholders, obligations and conflicts of interest (including the author’s) identified precisely.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Facts and unknowns separated; stakeholders and obligations mostly complete.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Facts and assumptions mixed; important stakeholders or conflicts missing.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Facts asserted without distinction; stakeholders listed without obligations.

rubric.criterion: Ethical analysis through two or more frameworks

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Two or more frameworks applied independently and accurately; disagreements identified and resolved with stated reasons; the strongest counterargument is engaged, not dismissed.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Two frameworks applied correctly; the counterargument is fair but treated briefly.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Frameworks named but used to decorate a conclusion already reached; counterargument weak.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No real ethical analysis, or a single framework presented as settling the question.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Performance across plausible futures assessed; irreversible elements identified; harms named with specific safeguards; who bears the downside is explicit.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Uncertainty and harms addressed with reasonable safeguards; reversibility noted.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Risks listed generically; safeguards vague.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Uncertainty ignored or presented as a single forecast.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Disclosure plan names audiences, timing and content; first steps are concrete; signposts and precommitted triggers are observable and tied to pre-agreed actions; review date set.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Disclosure and review covered with mostly specific triggers.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Disclosure or triggers vague (“we will monitor closely”).

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No disclosure plan or review mechanism.

prompts: Recall a decision in your career that you now see had an ethical dimension you did not notice at the time. Which enabler of ethical fading — euphemism, gradual steps, diffuse responsibility or self-image — was at work?
In the Executive Dilemma, which indicator did you protect first without deciding to? What does that suggest about your default under pressure from a powerful sponsor?
Which predictive tools or scoring systems in your work affect people with little power over the result? For one of them, could you name its target variable, its validator and its review date today?
Name one irreversible decision you expect to face in the next two years. Who will bear its downside, and what would you need to see to change course?

review.front: What are the four ethical questions this course uses to test a decision?
review.back: Consequences (who gains and loses, how likely), duties and rights (what is owed regardless of payoff), character (what a practically wise person would do and what it makes of us), and fairness (could the rule be justified to everyone affected).

review.front: What should you conclude when the four ethical questions disagree about a decision?
review.back: That you have found a genuine dilemma. Choose openly, state what you are trading and why — do not pick the framework that blesses your preferred option.

review.front: What is the accountability argument against stakeholder governance?
review.back: Leaders told to balance many constituencies with no trade-off rule can justify almost any decision and become harder to hold accountable to anyone; given their incentives, the discretion is unlikely to help stakeholders (Bebchuk and Tallarita).

review.front: What limits did Friedman place on profit-seeking in his 1970 essay?
review.back: Conformity to the basic rules of society in law and ethical custom, and open competition without deception or fraud.

review.front: Rank the remedies for a conflict of interest from weakest to strongest in typical effect.
review.back: Disclosure (weakest; people underestimate how interests bend judgment), recusal, restructuring the incentive, prohibition. Choice depends on stakes and on whether someone else can decide.
Systematic, often unconscious limits on ethical behavior: people predict, act and remember less ethically than they believe (Bazerman and Tenbrunsel).

review.front: Name the four enablers of ethical fading.
review.back: Euphemistic language, the slippery slope, errors in perceiving causation (diffused responsibility) and constraints from self-image (Tenbrunsel and Messick).

review.front: What did Welsh and colleagues find about gradual versus abrupt opportunities to cheat?
review.back: Gradually escalating opportunities led to more of the larger transgression than abrupt ones, through moral disengagement; a prevention focus weakened the effect.

review.front: What happened to the 2012 PNAS “signing at the beginning” study?
review.back: A large preregistered replication by the original authors and colleagues found no effect (2020), and PNAS retracted the paper in 2021 after evidence that its field data were invalid.

review.front: What are the three components of agency costs?
review.back: Monitoring costs borne by the principal, bonding costs borne by the agent, and the residual loss that remains (Jensen and Meckling).

review.front: Who most often brought corporate frauds to light in Dyck, Morse and Zingales’s study?
review.back: Non-traditional actors — employees, the media and industry regulators — more than investors, the SEC or auditors.

review.front: How did the healthcare algorithm studied by Obermeyer and colleagues produce racial bias?
review.back: It predicted health-care cost as a proxy for need; because less was spent on Black patients with the same need, equal scores hid unequal sickness. Changing the target reduced the bias.

review.front: What are the four core functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
review.back: Govern (cross-cutting policies, roles and accountability), Map (context and impacts), Measure (assess and track risks) and Manage (prioritize and act).

review.front: When does expected-value maximization work well?
review.back: When probabilities are reliable, the decision is repeated so averages are realized, no outcome is ruinous and the decision-maker bears the outcomes.

review.front: What do robust and adaptive approaches to deep uncertainty ask instead of “what will happen?”
review.back: Which strategy performs acceptably across many plausible futures, under what conditions it would fail, and which signposts and triggers will prompt pre-planned changes.

review.front: Why do irreversible decisions deserve extra care?
review.back: Irreversibility plus expected learning creates a value of keeping options open (Arrow and Fisher), and when others bear the downside, the duty and fairness questions weigh more heavily. Most decisions are reversible and should be made fast.

preview.text: Week 14 brings the semester together. Its lessons on presenting and defending decisions to skeptical senior audiences and on judging decisions without outcome bias complete the cycle this week begins: decide responsibly before the outcome is known, defend the decision honestly, then learn from what happened without hindsight. The decision memo you write this week is a direct rehearsal for the capstone defense, where a board will ask exactly the questions about harms, safeguards and accountability that this week trains.

links.why: Presenting and defending decisions, and after-action review without outcome bias, build on this week’s decision memo and premortem.
